newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- MAY 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- MAY 2.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Eight banks have declared themselves interested in the purchase of the Bank of Central Greece, indicating the high level of interest in the banking system and plans by financial credit institutions to expand into retail banking. The banks are Aspis, Ergobank, Egnatia, Euroinvestment, Europen Popular, bank of Piraeus, Bank of Cyprus and Bank of Nova Scotia.

--Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis will re-examine state lending with the aim of alleviating possible pressure on high borrowing needs in September, which will come close to the 1.7 trillion drachma mark. Sources say that the minister will attempt to increase the state's reserves in the months before September, bombarding the market with state titles between May and July.

--State inflows saw a significant improvement in April, with rates moving closer to the forecast target of an average 15.6 percent. According to estimates from the finance ministry, total inflows in April exceeded 600 billion drachmas.
--STET mobile phone subscribers are paying an extra 4.0 percent on their subscriptions as of yesterday while Panafon is set to increase rates as of May 12.
--'Objective tax criteria', high taxation rates on profits and the general crisis in the market is forcing many smaller businesses to close.

--The Athens Stock Exchange saw turnover of 1.3 trillion drachmas in the first four months of the year with the general price index rising 57.0 percent. The best returns came from banks, which saw an increase of 86.0 percent.

--The state's revenues in April were up by about 20.0 percent in April, according to the finance ministry, with the increase mainly attributed to increased activity by the finance ministry's taxation collection services - including the activity of the new SDOE economic crimes squad unit - and to returns of 60 billion drachmas in profits from telecoms organisation OTE and the Bank of Greece.

--Changes to the job market must be decided through social dialogue between the government, unions and employers by the end of October to allow implementation by next year, according to a decision reportedly taken during a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Costas Simitis yesterday.
--Ionian Bank is considering the option of rescheduling business debts, following the lead taken by the National Bank and the National Mortgage Bank, according to sources.
--Social dialogue will officially begin on May 14, it was decided yesterday at meeting of leading government and ruling PASOK party officials, chaired by the prime minister.
--Meanwhile, dissent in the labour movement led to the holding of three different rallies yesterday in Athens to celebrate Labour Day.

--Financial credit institutions operating as credit cooperatives will be permitted to call themselves "cooperative banks", the Bank of Greece clarified in a recent response to the Association of Greek Banks.

--An International Monetary Fund team of experts tomorrow begins its annual evaluation of the state of the Greek economy and finances, which will assist the government in making a substantial evaluation of the effectiveness of its policies in the first four months of the year. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
